TITLE¶

Loan Portfolio Analysis and Credit Risk Assessment Using Python¶

Objective¶

Analyze loan data to understand portfolio composition, identify data quality issues, explore default patterns, and evaluate factors associated with loan default.¶

Business Problem¶

The lending business needs to understand its loan portfolio, identify factors associated with loan defaults, and assess potential repayment risks. However, analyzing loan records without proper data cleaning and systematic analysis can make it difficult to identify patterns and support informed lending decisions.

The objective of this project is to analyze loan data to understand portfolio distribution, examine loan performance across different loan types, employment categories, and regions, and identify potential risk indicators. The analysis also evaluates the relationship between borrowers' credit scores, monthly income, loan amounts, interest rates, and EMI obligations.

Using Python, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Seaborn, the project aims to identify meaningful patterns, highlight potential data-quality issues, and provide actionable recommendations to support better credit risk assessment and lending decisions.

Handling Missing Values in Monthly Income and Credit Score¶

Monthly Income has 8 missing values, while Credit Score has 11 missing values.

I will use median imputation to handle these missing values because the median is less sensitive to extreme values than the mean. This approach allows me to retain the records for further analysis without deleting them.

However, the imputed values will be estimates and may affect the analysis of credit risk.

3.9 Outlier Detection in Loan Amount and EMI¶

In this section, I will identify potential outliers in Loan Amount and EMI using the Interquartile Range (IQR) method. This will help identify unusually high or low values that may require further investigation.

In [243]:
# Function to identify outliers using the IQR method
def detect_outliers(data, column):
    Q1 = data[column].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = data[column].quantile(0.75)

    IQR = Q3 - Q1

    lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

    outliers = data[
        (data[column] < lower_bound) |
        (data[column] > upper_bound)]

    print(f"\nColumn: {column}")
    print(f"Lower Bound: {lower_bound:.2f}")
    print(f"Upper Bound: {upper_bound:.2f}")
    print(f"Number of Outliers: {len(outliers)}")
    return outliers
# Detect outliers in both columns
loan_amount_outliers = detect_outliers(df, 'Loan Amount (INR)')
emi_outliers = detect_outliers(df, 'EMI (INR)')

Interpretation of Outlier Detection¶

The Interquartile Range (IQR) method identified 49 potential outliers in Loan Amount and 42 potential outliers in EMI.

The negative lower bounds are mathematical results of the IQR method and do not represent valid negative loan amounts or EMIs.

These observations require further investigation to determine whether they represent genuine high-value loans or data quality issues. The outliers will not be removed automatically because extreme values may contain important information for credit risk analysis.

In [253]:
# Calculate expected EMI using loan amount, interest rate, and tenure
P = df['Loan Amount (INR)']
r = df['Interest Rate (%)'] / 1200
n = df['Tenure (Months)']
df['Expected EMI (INR)'] = np.where(
    r == 0,
    P / n,
    P * r * (1 + r)**n / ((1 + r)**n - 1))

df['EMI Difference (INR)'] = (
    df['EMI (INR)'] - df['Expected EMI (INR)'])
display(
    df.nlargest(10, 'EMI (INR)')[

Findings from EMI Outlier Investigation¶

The comparison between recorded EMI and calculated EMI identified three records with substantial discrepancies.

Several other high EMI observations were consistent with the standard EMI formula, indicating that statistical outliers are not necessarily incorrect records.

The suspicious records have been flagged for further investigation. No values were automatically deleted or replaced because the original loan details must be verified before making corrections.

Findings from EMI Review¶

The EMI validation identified six records requiring further investigation. Five records showed extremely large percentage differences between recorded and expected EMI, while one record showed a smaller discrepancy.

These records have been flagged for review rather than automatically removed or modified. The original loan details should be verified before making any corrections.

Interpretation of Overall Default Rate¶

The analysis shows that 50 out of 760 loan records are classified as Defaulted or Written Off, resulting in an overall default rate of 6.58%.

This indicates that 6.58% of the loan records fall into these two categories. Further analysis is required to identify which loan types, employment categories, and credit score groups are associated with higher default rates.

      .sort_values(ascending=False))

# Create the chart
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
ax = default_rate_by_type.plot(kind='bar')
plt.title('Default Rate by Loan Type')
plt.xlabel('Loan Type')
plt.ylabel('Default Rate (%)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)


for container in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(container, fmt='%.2f%%', padding=3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation of Default Rate by Loan Type¶

The analysis shows that Business Loans have the highest observed default rate at 9.46% followed by Home Loans at 9.01%. Gold Loans have the lowest default rate at 4.44%.

Business and Home Loans may require closer risk assessment. However, the number of loans in each category should also be considered before making underwriting decisions.

more analysis of employment type and credit score may help identify additional patterns associated with default risk.

The analysis shows that customers with credit scores below 650 have the highest observed default rate of 11.57%.

Customers with scores between 650 and 749 have the lowest default rate at 3.87%, while customers scoring 750 and above have a default rate of 4.81%. These findings suggest that borrowers with lower credit scores may require closer credit risk assessment. However, further analysis of group sizes and other financial factors is necessary before recommending changes to lending criteria.

    linewidths=0.5)
plt.title('Correlation Heatmap of Loan Variables')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation¶

The correlation heatmap shows the relationships between Credit Score, Monthly Income, Loan Amount, Interest Rate, and EMI.

Key observations:

Loan Amount and EMI (0.37): These variables have a moderate positive correlation. Larger loans tend to be associated with higher monthly EMIs. Interest Rate and EMI (0.20): There is a weak positive correlation, indicating that higher interest rates tend to be associated with higher EMIs. Monthly Income and Interest Rate (-0.06): This is a very weak negative correlation, suggesting almost no linear relationship between these variables in this dataset. Credit Score and Monthly Income (0.08): These variables have a very weak positive correlation. Credit Score and EMI (0.02): The correlation is almost zero, indicating virtually no linear relationship between these variables. Overall observation: Most pairs have weak linear correlations. Loan Amount and EMI have the strongest positive correlation among the pairs shown.

Conclusion: Loan Amount has the clearest positive relationship with EMI in this dataset. However, correlation does not imply causation, and these values do not establish whether a variable causes loan defaults.

The multi-panel visualization presents the distribution of loans across four regions and six loan types.

Key observations:

Regional distribution: East has the highest number of loans, with approximately 205. North follows with around 188, while South and West have approximately 184 loans each. Loan type distribution: Business Loans represent the largest category, with approximately 148 loans. Gold and Personal Loans: Gold Loans account for approximately 135 loans, followed by Personal Loans with approximately 134. Smaller loan categories: Auto Loans, Education Loans, and Home Loans have comparatively fewer records. Conclusion: These charts provide an overview of portfolio composition and help identify the regions and loan types contributing the most loans. Loan counts alone do not indicate profitability or credit risk.

Findings: Default Rate by Loan Type¶

The bar chart compares the default rates across six loan types.

Business Loans have the highest default rate at 9.46%, indicating a greater observed risk of default compared with the other loan categories. Home Loans have the second-highest default rate at 9.01%, suggesting that this category also deserves closer risk assessment. Personal Loans have a default rate of 5.97%, followed by Education Loans at 5.26%. Auto Loans have a default rate of 5.08%, while Gold Loans have the lowest rate at 4.44%. The difference between the highest and lowest default rates is approximately 5.02 percentage points, highlighting variations in default outcomes across loan types.

Conclusion: Business Loans and Home Loans have the highest observed default rates, while Gold Loans have the lowest. The lending team should investigate the factors associated with higher default rates in Business and Home Loans and consider additional creditworthiness checks for these categories.

Key Findings and Business Recommendations¶

Key Findings¶

  1. Overall default rate

The dataset contains 760 loans, of which 50 are classified as Defaulted or Written Off. The overall default rate is approximately 6.58%.

  1. Default rates vary by loan type

Business Loans have the highest observed default rate at 9.46%, followed by Home Loans at 9.01%. These categories warrant further investigation to understand the factors associated with their higher default rates.

  1. Credit score is associated with default outcomes

Borrowers with credit scores below 650 have an observed default rate of 11.57%, compared with 3.87% for the 650–750 group and 4.81% for the above-750 group. The lowest credit-score group has the highest observed default rate, although the pattern is not strictly decreasing across all groups.

  1. Employment category differences

Salaried customers have an observed default rate of 8.49%, compared with 6.84% for Self-Employed customers and 4.31% for Business Owners. These are associations in the current dataset, not evidence that employment type itself causes defaults.

  1. Potential affordability concerns

The EMI-to-income ratio has a median of approximately 22.80% and a mean of approximately 43.90%. The mean is substantially higher than the median, suggesting a right-skewed distribution with unusually high ratios. Some records should be checked for data-quality issues before drawing conclusions about affordability.

  1. High-risk loan identification

Using the illustrative rule of Credit Score below 650 and EMI-to-income ratio above 40%, the analysis identifies 72 high-risk loans, including 45 currently Active loans. These records could be prioritized for further review.

Underwriting Recommendation

Introduce an additional affordability and creditworthiness review for applicants with low credit scores and high EMI-to-income ratios. Review the 45 currently Active loans flagged by the rule, verify unusually high EMI values and income records, and evaluate whether the proposed thresholds are appropriate before using them in lending decisions.

The thresholds should be validated against historical repayment outcomes before being adopted as formal underwriting policy.
